assumptionReview.assumption: Cap default values: maxParts=10_000, maxHeadersPerPart=100, maxHeaderBytesPerPart=16_384, maxPartBytes=undefined (no cap). Defaults applied at validation-time via `?? <DEFAULT>` after validatePositiveTimeout so values stay fixed for the operation's lifetime.
assumptionReview.rationale: Verified at src/parse-multipart-related.ts:231-234 by Read. Defaults match the planner's technicalNotes table verbatim and align with review-security.md F-S-001/004/012 recommendations. The closure-scoped resolved values (`maxParts`, `maxHeadersPerPart`, `maxHeaderBytesPerPart`) are referenced by the listeners NOT `opts.*` directly — eliminates the race-on-opts-mutation concern raised in the alternatives. maxPartBytes intentionally has no default per the security-review (per-part concern depends on application). The behavior shift from Sprint 1-5 (omitted == no cap) to Sprint 6 (omitted == safe defaults) is documented in JSDoc and is the right call per the security review. T-081b (omitted maxParts admits 5-part envelope) verifies the omitted-case path doesn't false-trip.

assumptionReview.assumption: Header-bytes measurement formula: `Buffer.byteLength(name) + 4 + measureHeaderValueBytes(value)` per logical header line. The `+4` is `': '` (2 bytes) + `'\r\n'` (2 bytes) — on-the-wire framing per RFC 7230 §3.2. For repeated values, charge N × (nameBytes + 4) + sum(value bytes).
assumptionReview.rationale: Verified at src/parse-multipart-related.ts:401-410. Deterministic, conservative under-count (SOFT cap — under-count is safe per the documented contract), and matches the on-the-wire framing an attacker would care about. measureHeaderValueBytes (lines 102-117) recurses through string/array/Buffer with sensible 0 fallback for forward-compat shapes (Buffer/Buffer[]/Buffer[][] from the ambient shim). The alternative of using flattenDicerHeaders would join repeats with `, ` per RFC 7230 (different from per-repeat framing), so the choice not to reuse it is correct for the cap semantics. T-076(b) verifies the formula trips at 16384 with a 32 KiB value.

assumptionReview.assumption: T-081b 10_001-part envelope explicit overflow test elided. Default-application contract verified instead via (a) omitted maxParts admits 5-part envelope (no false-positive at default boundary) AND (b) explicit maxParts:1 trips on 2nd part with observed:2 (proves off-by-one boundary semantics that the default also uses).
assumptionReview.rationale: The 10_001-part envelope test would be slow (hundreds of ms to build buffer + parse) for marginal coverage value over the boundary semantics test. The off-by-one semantics that the default uses are exercised by maxParts:1 (cheap and conclusive). The literal default value is also asserted at the JSDoc layer + the omitted-case test admits-5-parts contract. Better than the alternatives (it.skipIf(CI) adds CI-conditional logic; smaller envelope + patched default would defeat the test). Slight RISK that a bug in the default-resolution `?? 10_000` (e.g. `?? 10` typo) wouldn't be caught — but the explicit value at parse-multipart-related.ts:232 is a single literal and would be caught by the JSDoc cross-reference + a future Sprint 7 hardening test. assumptionReview.assumption: Cap-trip behavior pattern for maxPartBytes: (1) destroy upstream partStream to stop dicer pumping; (2) push MultipartPartTooLargeError into queue (FIRST item next .next() sees); (3) end counter cleanly via counter.end() so consumer's CURRENT in-flight drain on `body` resolves naturally — without step 3, consumer sees 'Premature close' BEFORE typed error has a chance to surface.
assumptionReview.rationale: Verified at src/parse-multipart-related.ts:489-515 by Read. The ordering (destroy upstream → signalError → end counter) is exactly what the assumption documents. The `if (counter.writableEnded)` guard at line 507 prevents double-end. The `if (counter.writable && !counter.writableEnded)` guard at line 512 prevents 'write after end'. The `if (tripped) return` short-circuit at line 490 prevents double-fire on subsequent chunks (verified by T-075 streaming test at parse-resource-caps.test.ts:120-162). Could lose the typed error to a race with truncation detection (Sprint 3) or abort handling (Sprint 4) only if those fire BEFORE the cap-trip — but the queue is first-fire-wins and the cap fires synchronously inside the partStream 'data' listener, so under a normal envelope with a too-large part the cap-trip wins. Empirically validated by 9 cap-trip tests in parse-resource-caps + 4 in fetch-resource-caps.

assumptionReview.assumption: PassThrough vs direct 'data' listener for maxPartBytes — generator chose PassThrough to avoid an EventEmitter snapshot race where pipe's internal data listener fires AFTER trip+unpipe (because the listener array was snapshotted at the start of emit()), surfacing 'write after end'. PassThrough buffers writes when downstream isn't reading, so consumer's later listener attach catches every byte.
assumptionReview.rationale: Verified at src/parse-multipart-related.ts:470-532 by Read. The chosen pattern (PassThrough + explicit 'data'/'end'/'error' bridge instead of pipe) is sound and the generator's reasoning (EventEmitter snapshot race; consumer attach race window after dicer pumps body bytes synchronously after 'header' emit) is correct. The PassThrough is added to `allPartStreams` at line 481 so cleanup() at line 690-692 destroys it on every termination path. Per-part listeners (`onUpstreamData/End/Error` at lines 489-530) are attached to partStream which itself is destroyed in cleanup — listeners are released by destroy. Acceptable: the chosen pattern is documented (assumption #3) with empirical justification (initial direct-listener implementation timed out due to the race), and the alternative comparisons are concrete and correct.

assumptionReview.assumption: On overflow, both destroy upstream AND end counter cleanly (NOT counter.destroy(error)) — destroying the counter mid-drain surfaces 'Premature close' before our typed error has a chance to surface; ending cleanly lets the consumer's drain complete naturally so the iterator's next .next() resolves with our error.
assumptionReview.rationale: Verified at src/parse-multipart-related.ts:494-507 by Read. The ordering (destroy upstream → push error → end counter) is exactly what the assumption documents and matches the spec contract that the iterator surfaces the typed error (NOT the parser's body drain). Empirically verified by 9 cap-trip tests in parse-resource-caps.test.ts that successfully `expect(caught).toBeInstanceOf(MultipartPartTooLargeError)` — without this ordering, the tests would fail with 'Premature close' assertions. The alternative (counter.destroy(typed error)) would surface the error from the parser's catch site, NOT from the iterator's next .next() — wrong contract per spec/api.md.

suggestions.description: The per-part `onUpstreamData/End/Error` listeners attached to partStream when maxPartBytes is set are NOT explicitly removed by name in cleanup(). The `partStream.destroy()` call in the cleanup loop at line 690-692 detaches them implicitly (Node Readable destroy semantics), but a future hardening pass could attach via a single `removeListenerBundle` for symmetry with the source/dicer cleanup pattern at lines 653-655. Cosmetic — does not affect correctness; T-075 streaming test verifies no double-fire after trip via the `tripped` flag short-circuit.
